query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element NiCoFeCrAlX alloys, high-temperature oxidation resistance and retention of mechanical integrity are governed primarily by whether nanoscale B2-ordered Al-rich precipitates (<50 nm) persist at the metal/oxide interface; these precipitates act as local Al reservoirs that (i) sustain the growth of a slow-growing, adherent α-Al2O3 scale and (ii) pin grain boundaries, suppressing void formation that would otherwise debond the scale. If the precipitates dissolve or coarsen beyond ≈150 nm, Al is no longer replenished locally, oxidation accelerates, and scale spallation and intergranular cracking increase.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic (Ni,Co,Fe,Cr,Al) single-phase FCC alloy produced by arc-melting and homogenized at 1200 °C/24 h, then water-quenched. Grain size ≈30 µm; no long-range ordering detectable by XRD.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical aging schedule that either (A) promotes stable nanoscale B2 Al-rich precipitates (age at 750 °C/50 h, air cool) or (B) over-ages to coarsen/dissolve them (age at 1050 °C/50 h, furnace cool).
generation.conditions: Static laboratory air, 1100 °C isothermal hold for up to 500 h with 25 °C/min cyclic cooling every 24 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Density, size distribution, and interface continuity of B2 Al-rich precipitates at the metal/oxide interface (quantified by TEM and 3-D atom probe).
generation.mechanism: Stable nanoscale precipitates provide short-range fast-diffusion sources of Al that continuously feed the growing oxide without long-distance bulk diffusion. Their coherent interfaces also impede vacancy condensation and boundary grooving, maintaining scale adhesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Variant (A) will (1) show parabolic oxidation kinetics with k_p ≈ 1×10⁻¹³–3×10⁻¹³ g² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (≥5× slower than baseline), (2) retain ≥95 % scale coverage after 20 thermal cycles, and (3) exhibit <2 % loss in room-temperature tensile strength. Variant (B) will approach baseline behavior (k_p ≥1×10⁻¹² g² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹), suffer ≥30 % scale spallation, and lose >10 % tensile strength due to internal oxidation and grain-boundary voiding.
generation.baseline: Same alloy composition tested directly after homogenization (no Al-rich precipitates; single-phase FCC).
generation.boundary: Expected to hold for dry air or Ar–20 %O₂ between 900–1200 °C and total Al content 6–12 at %; fails if Al <6 at % or if water vapor >10 % (scale volatility dominates).
generation.uncertainty: 1. Exact precipitate size threshold for effectiveness may vary (±30 nm). 2. Possible synergistic effects of minor elements (e.g., Y, Si) are not captured. 3. Long-term (>2000 h) stability not yet evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three coupon sets: baseline (FCC), variant A (750 °C aged), variant B (1050 °C aged). Expose all to 1100 °C cyclic oxidation for 500 h. Record mass change every 24 h; cross-section each coupon after 250 h and 500 h for TEM/EDS mapping of oxide scale and precipitate morphology; perform room-temperature tensile tests pre- and post-exposure.
measurements: Mass-gain vs time to obtain k_p
Percentage of intact oxide scale after cooling (image analysis)
Precipitate size distribution at metal/oxide interface (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variant A does NOT show significantly lower k_p (≤50 % difference from baseline) AND fails to maintain ≥80 % scale coverage OR loses >10 % tensile strength, the hypothesis is falsified.
